blocks.content: Manipur's economy reflects its valley-hills geography (Chapter 1) — wet-rice cultivation dominates the fertile valley, while shifting/terrace cultivation and forest-produce livelihoods characterise the hill economy, alongside a globally significant sporting-goods manufacturing niche.

items: Rice is overwhelmingly the dominant crop of the Imphal Valley, grown through both traditional and modern irrigation methods, forming the backbone of the state's food economy.

In the hill districts, a mix of terrace cultivation and, in more remote areas, traditional shifting ('jhum') cultivation continues to be practised, alongside horticulture (oranges, pineapples and other fruits well-suited to the hill climate).

Manipur is notably one of India's significant producers of certain niche horticultural products, including specific varieties of chilli (such as the very high-pungency 'Naga/Bhut Jolokia', associated with the wider North-East region including parts of Manipur) and black rice ('Chak-hao'), a distinctive, aromatic pigmented rice variety traditionally used in Manipuri festive dishes and increasingly marketed nationally as a premium/health-food product.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Chak-hao (Manipur black rice) is a distinctive GI-tagged agricultural product frequently tested as a state-specific economic-geography fact — remember it is a traditionally significant, aromatic, pigmented rice variety, now marketed nationally as a premium product.

Manipur has a globally notable, if geographically concentrated, sporting-goods manufacturing tradition, particularly for polo equipment (given Manipur's historic claim as the birthplace of modern polo, Chapter 9) and other sporting items.

Handloom weaving is a historically and economically significant traditional craft across Manipur, particularly associated with Meitei women weavers producing distinctive textiles including the 'Moirang Phee' and various traditional Manipuri sarong-style garments ('Phanek'), alongside similarly rich hill-community weaving traditions among Naga and Kuki-Zo groups, each with distinct traditional patterns and techniques.

items: Moreh, on the Manipur-Myanmar border, is a significant border-trade town, serving as one of India's key official land-trade points with Myanmar under the India-Myanmar Border Trade Agreement, and as a gateway for the wider India-ASEAN connectivity vision (linked to projects such as the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway).

This Myanmar-border trade and connectivity role gives Manipur's economy (and broader strategic significance) a distinctive 'Act East Policy' dimension, tying the state's economic development prospects to India's wider South-East Asian connectivity and trade ambitions.
Rice dominates Imphal Valley agriculture; hill districts practise terrace and shifting ('jhum') cultivation, plus horticulture.
Chak-hao (Manipur black rice) = distinctive GI-tagged aromatic pigmented rice variety.
Manipur has a notable sporting-goods (especially polo equipment) and handloom-weaving manufacturing tradition (Phanek, Moirang Phee).
Moreh (Manipur-Myanmar border) = key India-Myanmar border-trade town, linked to the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and India's Act East Policy.
